options.text: As an indication for intralipid, because any value above 12% is associated with fewer live births.
options.why: 12% is the arbitrary cut-off some clinics use, with no supporting basis: ESHRE recommends neither the test nor intralipid.

options.text: As a value within the wide range seen in healthy people (5–25%), with arbitrary cut-offs and different from uterine findings.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE does not recommend peripheral blood immune testing (“not recommended”).

options.text: As a result requiring a repeat study with uterine NK biopsy before the next transfer.
options.why: Uterine NK testing is also “not recommended”.

options.text: As a value that is only relevant if confirmed in two measurements one cycle apart.
options.why: There is no such criterion: the problem is the test itself, not its repetition.

items.explanation: Neither blood nor uterine NK cells predict live birth, and treating a “high” value exposes the patient to risks without proven benefit.

items.stem: A patient with diagnosed antiphospholipid syndrome (fictional case) starts IVF. How do the ESHRE recommendations on immunological add-ons apply?

options.text: They require stopping any immunological treatment during IVF, because all are “not recommended”.
options.why: That section does not refer to patients already treated for an autoimmune disease or another indication.

options.text: They indicate adding intralipid and IVIG preventively, because they have shown benefit in autoimmunity.
options.why: The recommendations do not report benefit of intralipid or IVIG in autoimmunity; that scenario is outside their scope.

options.text: They do not refer to her: the section excludes women with autoimmune disease, in whom the disease itself is treated.
options.why: Correct: the section excludes thyroid autoimmunity, antiphospholipid syndrome and immunotherapy for another indication.

options.text: They require testing her uterine NK cells and KIR/HLA genotype before deciding on antiphospholipid syndrome treatment.
options.why: These tests are, respectively, “not recommended” and “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”.

items.explanation: The recommendations against immune tests and treatments concern their use as add-ons, not the treatment of a diagnosed disease.

items.stem: A patient with low ovarian reserve (fictional case) asks about “ovarian rejuvenation” with intraovarian PRP. What evidence does ESHRE describe?

options.text: Two RCTs with more live births in low responders, so ESHRE classifies it as “can be considered”.
options.why: There is no RCT of intraovarian PRP; ESHRE's phrase is “not recommended”.

options.text: A meta-analysis of 7 studies with more clinical pregnancy (RR 1.79), though with small, heterogeneous samples.
options.why: These data correspond to intrauterine PRP, not intraovarian PRP.

options.text: No RCT: one case-control study and uncontrolled studies (696 women), with no safety data.
options.why: Correct: there are no safety data on injection into the ovarian stroma, and ESHRE does not recommend it.

options.text: A moderate-quality Cochrane review with no effect on live birth but a good long-term safety profile.
options.why: No such review of RCTs exists, and safety data are precisely what is missing.

items.explanation: The honest conversation with low reserve is about evidence-based options, including oocyte donation.

items.stem: On intrauterine G-CSF and stem cells, which statement is correct according to ESHRE and the NICE NG257 text?

options.text: G-CSF: possible benefit with low certainty, no difference in implantation failure; NICE NG257 does not address them specifically.
options.why: Correct: in implantation failure, RR 1.43 (95% CI 0.86–2.36); both are “not recommended” by ESHRE.

options.text: G-CSF: more live births with high certainty, so it is “recommended” for thin endometrium; NICE advises against it.
options.why: Certainty was low, the phrase is “not recommended” and NICE NG257 has no specific recommendation.

options.text: Stem cells: small RCTs with good results in premature ovarian insufficiency; NICE says not to offer them.
options.why: There are no RCTs of stem cells (only case reports and uncontrolled or very small studies), and NICE NG257 has no specific recommendation.

options.text: Stem cells: “can be considered” given their biological rationale; NICE recommends them within registered clinical trials.
options.why: ESHRE classifies them as “not recommended” because of serious safety concerns, including tumorigenesis risk.

items.explanation: NICE NG257 having no specific recommendation is not the same as advising against: it simply does not address them; the explicit position is ESHRE's.

items.stem: What do ESHRE and NICE say about screening hysteroscopy before IVF?

options.text: ESHRE recommends it before the first IVF in all patients; NICE says to offer it only after two failed good-quality transfers.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend it routinely, and NICE sets no such criterion of failed transfers.

options.text: Both consider it “not recommended” in any situation, including suspected uterine pathology or recurrent implantation failure.
options.why: NICE refers to investigation if abnormalities are suspected, and ESHRE allows it as an option in recurrent implantation failure.

options.text: NICE recommends it in recurrent implantation failure and after a previous miscarriage; ESHRE does not address screening hysteroscopy.
options.why: It is ESHRE that contemplates it in recurrent implantation failure (“can be considered”).

options.text: ESHRE: not routinely, but “can be considered” in recurrent implantation failure; NICE: do not offer it as pretreatment unless abnormalities are suspected.
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.40.2 refers to investigation of uterine abnormalities if they are suspected.

items.explanation: Both advise against systematic screening; they differ in the room they leave for specific groups.

items.stem: On endometrial scratching, which set of positions of the ESHRE add-ons document (2023), the ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline (2023) and NICE NG257 is correct?

options.text: Add-ons: “not recommended”; unexplained: probably not (conditional, ⊕); NICE: consider it after a failure.
options.why: All three positions are altered: the add-ons phrase, the strength of the unexplained guideline and NICE's.

options.text: Add-ons: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”; unexplained: do not offer (strong, ⊕⊕); NICE: do not offer (1.40.1).
options.why: Correct: none supports routine use; the difference lies in the strength of the phrase.

options.text: Add-ons: “can be considered”; unexplained: no statement; NICE: do not offer as pretreatment.
options.why: The add-ons phrase is a different one and the unexplained guideline does make a statement (rec. 45, strong, ⊕⊕).

options.text: Add-ons: “recommended” after previous failure; unexplained: should not be offered (strong, ⊕⊕); NICE: no recommendation.
options.why: The add-ons document does not recommend it in any group and NICE does have a recommendation (1.40.1).

items.explanation: If one guideline says “not routinely” and another “do not offer”, neither supports routine use: what changes is the room they leave for research or specific groups.

aemps-2024-genotonorm-intrarosa.title: Fichas técnicas de Genotonorm (somatropina) e Intrarosa 6,5 mg óvulos (prasterona)
aemps-2024-genotonorm-intrarosa.population: Growth disorders and growth hormone deficiency; postmenopausal vulvovaginal atrophy (Spain).
aemps-2024-genotonorm-intrarosa.finding: Genotonorm: paediatric growth and GH deficiency indications; none in reproduction. Intrarosa: moderate to severe postmenopausal vulvovaginal atrophy; the only prasterone (DHEA) listed in CIMA.
aemps-2024-genotonorm-intrarosa.limitations: The start of section 4.1 of one somatropin (SmPC dated 20 June 2024) out of 45 CIMA presentations was read. Intrarosa: https://cima.aemps.es/cima/dochtml/ft/1171255001/FT_1171255001.html.

eshre-2023-addons.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine
eshre-2023-addons.authors: ESHRE Add-ons Working Group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, Ebner T, Harper J, Le Clef N, Moffett A, Norcross S, Polyzos NP, Rautakallio-Hokkanen S, Sfontouris I, Sermon K, Vermeulen N, Pinborg A
eshre-2023-addons.population: Patients undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART); Hum Reprod 2023 (ESHRE Pages).
eshre-2023-addons.finding: 42 recommendations using its own four-phrase scale (recommended; can be considered; currently not recommended for routine clinical use; not recommended). Peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing: not recommended. Screening hysteroscopy: currently not recommended for routine clinical use (can be considered in recurrent implantation failure). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping: currently not recommended for routine clinical use. ICSI for non-male factor infertility: not recommended.
eshre-2023-addons.limitations: Full text read (UCL Discovery open-access copy of the advance online version); the wording of every cited recommendation and the scale-definition table were checked verbatim. Good practice recommendations based on review and consensus, not a GRADE guideline: no recommendation rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. ART population, not specifically unexplained infertility.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty). ICSI not recommended over conventional IVF (rec. 42, strong, ⊕); endometrial scratching should not be offered (rec. 45, strong, ⊕⊕); adjunct oral antioxidants in women probably not recommended (rec. 46, conditional, ⊕).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.title: Ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI — ESHRE guideline update 2025
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Ovarian Stimulation
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.population: Women starting ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI.
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.finding: Recommends AFC or AMH to predict high and low response (strong). Does not recommend AFC, AMH or other basal markers to predict pregnancy or live birth (strong). Female age and BMI are predictors of pregnancy and live birth (strong). Age, BMI, basal FSH, inhibin B, basal oestradiol, basal progesterone and basal LH are not recommended to predict response (strong). Adjuncts (recs 46–53): growth hormone not recommended in normal responders (strong, ⊕) or PCOS (strong, ⊕⊕), probably not recommended in low responders (conditional, ⊕); testosterone probably not recommended in low responders (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕); DHEA not recommended in low or normal responders (strong, ⊕⊕); aspirin (strong, ⊕⊕⊕) and sildenafil in low responders (strong, ⊕) not recommended.
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.limitations: Full guideline v23 (September 2026); journal version: Hum Reprod 2026;41(4):498-514. Certainty for each recommendation is given in the full guideline.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse. Unexplained fertility problems: keep trying for 2 years in total before treatment (1.38.1); do not offer ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2); then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.38.3). Male factor: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally at 3 months (1.17.4); do not test sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer androgens (1.24.3). Endometriosis: expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgery; then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.36.1–1.36.3). Add-ons: do not offer endometrial scratch or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment (1.40.1–1.40.2), endometrial receptivity testing (1.41.1), immunological agents (1.42.1) or PGT-A (1.48.1); do not offer assisted hatching (1.49.1, from 2004); ICSI: offer with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes, consider with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation, and do not use without male factor (1.50.1–1.50.5).
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
